analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from asking job applicants for their salary history or using it to set pay.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it unlawful under federal wage law for an employer to screen job applicants based on their past pay, to ask an applicant's current or former employer what they earned, or to retaliate against workers who complain about those practices. Employers who violated it would face civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation and could owe each affected applicant up to $10,000 in damages plus attorneys' fees [S2][S3]. The idea is that when a new job offer is anchored to whatever someone was paid before, past pay discrimination and underpayment follow workers from job to job, which hits women and minority workers hardest [S1].
analysis.who_benefits: Job applicants whose previous pay was low relative to their skills — disproportionately women and minority workers, whose lower past earnings would otherwise be carried forward as a baseline for future offers. Workers who would otherwise face retaliation for objecting to salary-history questions also gain a private right to sue with damages and attorneys' fees [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Job seekers, especially women and minority workers

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits employers from screening applicants based on previous wages or salary histories, including by requiring disclosure as a condition of an interview or an offer [S3].
Prohibits employers from seeking an applicant's pay history from current or former employers, cutting off one channel through which past underpayment is carried into new job offers [S3].

Makes retaliation against employees or applicants who oppose or complain about these practices unlawful, and gives victims up to $10,000 in special damages plus attorneys' fees, with civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation for employers [S3].
Because pay offers are often anchored to prior salary, removing salary history from hiring is aimed at stopping the compounding of past wage discrimination across careers [S1].

analysis.who_pays: Employers lose a cheap and widely used screening tool: salary history. They would face federal penalties and civil damages if they keep asking, and hiring managers would need to replace salary-history screening with other ways of setting and verifying offers. Recruiters and background-check firms that supply salary verification would lose a product line. Supporters of the status quo argue employers use salary history to gauge expectations and experience, not only to lowball workers, and that the change adds compliance cost and litigation risk [S3].

drawbacks.text: Employers legitimately use salary history for purposes other than anchoring pay — verifying experience, gauging seniority, and checking honesty on resumes — and the bill would remove that information entirely, raising compliance and litigation costs [S3].

The penalties are per violation and the bill allows class-style actions brought by one applicant on behalf of others similarly situated, which critics would call a litigation magnet for staffing agencies and high-volume employers [S3].

Salary history is not the only driver of the pay gap, so the bill's effect on wage inequality depends on how much employers actually anchor offers to prior pay — a mechanism the bill asserts rather than proves [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to job seekers is real but narrower than the headline: it removes one practice that can carry past underpayment forward, rather than directly raising anyone's pay. The cost to employers is mostly friction — retraining hiring processes and bearing litigation risk — and modest relative to the potential gains for workers whose prior pay was unfairly low. States and cities that have adopted similar bans have kept them, which suggests employers adapt.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 2016 and referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017 [S5][S1].

narrative.text: Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton introduced the Pay Equity for All Act of 2016 in the House on September 14, 2016, with Reps. Nadler, DeLauro, and Speier as original cosponsors [S3].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce — the full extent of its action history [S5].
It attracted 25 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors, and the Republican-majority committee never held a hearing or markup on it [S4][S1].
No vote was ever taken in either chamber, and the bill expired at the end of the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers keep their ability to ask applicants and previous employers for salary history without federal penalties. Underpaid workers, disproportionately women, got no relief: past pay discrimination continued to follow them into future job offers, as it does under current law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers kept salary-history screening without penalty

industries.note: Employers would lose the ability to screen and anchor offers using an applicant's past pay, facing civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation and damages of up to $10,000 per affected applicant. That information is often the cheapest way to keep wage offers low, which is exactly why supporters say past underpayment compounds.
Firms that supply salary verification to recruiters would lose that business, since seeking an applicant's pay history from current or former employers would become unlawful.

Agencies make heavy use of salary history to price candidates and would bear compliance costs and litigation exposure under the per-violation penalty structure, but they are not the bill's only target and some would gain credibility with candidates.
